source: Period boundaries: ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart v2023/09. Climate numbers per turn come from climate_history.json.

ages.description: Animal life diversifies explosively in the seas: the Cambrian explosion produces nearly all modern animal phyla. The land is bare rock and microbial crust.
keyEvents: Cambrian explosion (~539–515 Ma): most animal phyla appear in the fossil record
Burgess Shale and Chengjiang biotas preserve soft-bodied animals
Trilobites become the dominant arthropods
First chordates and jawless vertebrates (e.g. Haikouichthys)
End-Cambrian extinction pulses (biomere events) hit trilobites
ages.vegetation: None on land: bare rock with microbial mats

environmentalConditions.seaLevel: High and rising; shallow seas flood the continents
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Gondwana in the south; Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia as separate continents

ages.description: Marine life multiplies in the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event and the first plants creep onto land. The period ends in an ice age and one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions.
keyEvents: Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event: marine genera roughly triple
First land plants: spores of liverwort-like plants (~470 Ma)
Early reefs built by corals, sponges and bryozoans; nautiloids are top predators
Gondwana drifts over the South Pole
Hirnantian glaciation (~445 Ma) and the Late Ordovician mass extinction (~85% of species)
ages.vegetation: First non-vascular, liverwort-like plants near water

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Greenhouse, then a sharp ice age at the end
environmentalConditions.seaLevel: Among the highest in Earth history, then a ~100 m glacial drop
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Gondwana over the South Pole; small continents in the tropics

ages.description: Life recovers in warm, shallow seas. Vascular plants and the first land animals gain a foothold, and jawed fishes spread.
keyEvents: First vascular plants such as Cooksonia (~430 Ma)
First land animals: millipedes and other arthropods
Jawed fishes (placoderms, acanthodians) diversify
Giant sea scorpions (eurypterids) and extensive coral reefs
Laurentia and Baltica collide, raising the Caledonian mountains
ages.vegetation: Small vascular plants along wet lowlands

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Warm; mostly ice-free after early glacial phases
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Euramerica (Laurussia) forms; Gondwana in the south

ages.description: The 'Age of Fishes'. The first forests transform the land and the atmosphere, and the first four-limbed vertebrates crawl ashore. Two extinction pulses end the period.
keyEvents: Fishes diversify: armored placoderms, early sharks and lobe-finned fishes
First trees and forests (Archaeopteris, ~385 Ma); first seed plants late in the period
Tetrapods evolve from lobe-finned fish (Tiktaalik ~375 Ma, Acanthostega ~365 Ma)
Insects appear on land
Late Devonian extinction (Kellwasser ~372 Ma, Hangenberg ~359 Ma) collapses reef ecosystems
ages.vegetation: First forests and deep soils; plants spread inland

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Warm, cooling toward glaciation at the end
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Euramerica near the equator, Gondwana to the south

ages.description: Vast swamp forests bury the carbon that becomes coal. Oxygen reaches its all-time high, arthropods grow to giant sizes, and ice sheets spread over southern Gondwana.
keyEvents: Coal swamp forests of giant lycopsids (Lepidodendron) and tree ferns
Atmospheric oxygen peaks (est. 30–35%)
Giant arthropods: Meganeura dragonflies (~70 cm wingspan), Arthropleura millipedes
First amniotes (Hylonomus, ~312 Ma): eggs that no longer need water
Late Paleozoic Ice Age; Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse (~305 Ma)
ages.vegetation: Dense swamp forests across the tropics

environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Pangaea assembling as Euramerica and Gondwana collide

ages.description: Pangaea is complete. Its interior dries out, mammal ancestors (synapsids) dominate the land, and the period ends with the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.
keyEvents: Pangaea fully assembled, with vast arid interiors
Synapsids dominate: Dimetrodon, then therapsids (mammal ancestors)
Conifers and other seed plants replace the coal-swamp floras
The Late Paleozoic Ice Age ends in the early Permian
Siberian Traps eruptions trigger the Permian–Triassic extinction (~252 Ma): ~80% of marine species lost
ages.vegetation: Conifers, cycads and seed ferns; deserts inland

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Icehouse early, extreme hothouse at the end
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Pangaea: one supercontinent in the Panthalassa ocean

ages.description: Life slowly recovers in a hot, dry world. Dinosaurs, pterosaurs and the first mammal relatives appear, and a mass extinction at the end clears the way for the dinosaurs.
keyEvents: Slow recovery from the 'Great Dying'
First dinosaurs (~233–230 Ma), pterosaurs and marine reptiles such as ichthyosaurs
First mammaliaforms (~225 Ma)
Carnian Pluvial Episode (~234 Ma): a wet phase lasting about a million years
Central Atlantic Magmatic Province eruptions cause the end-Triassic extinction (~201 Ma)
ages.vegetation: Conifers, cycads and ginkgoes; ferns along rivers

environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Pangaea begins to rift; strong 'megamonsoon' seasons

ages.description: Pangaea splits apart and warm, humid conditions spread. Dinosaurs dominate the land, giant sauropods roam, and the first birds take flight.
keyEvents: Pangaea splits into Laurasia and Gondwana; the Atlantic begins to open
Giant sauropods (Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus) and large theropods (Allosaurus)
First birds (Archaeopteryx, ~150 Ma) evolve from feathered dinosaurs
Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs rule the seas; ammonites flourish
Gymnosperm forests of conifers, cycads and ginkgoes
ages.vegetation: Lush gymnosperm forests and fern prairies

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Warm and humid; little or no polar ice
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Laurasia in the north, Gondwana in the south

ages.description: A greenhouse world with very high seas. Flowering plants appear and spread, dinosaurs reach their peak, and an asteroid impact ends the era.
keyEvents: Flowering plants appear (~130 Ma) and spread worldwide alongside pollinating insects
Greenhouse peak in the Cenomanian–Turonian (~94 Ma); no permanent polar ice
Shallow seas flood the continents (e.g. the Western Interior Seaway)
Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops and other famous dinosaurs (Late Cretaceous)
Chicxulub asteroid impact (66 Ma): ~75% of species, including all non-avian dinosaurs, die out
ages.vegetation: Flowering plants spread; first grasses late in the period

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Very warm, among the warmest of the last 500 million years
environmentalConditions.seaLevel: Very high (up to ~200 m above today)
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Gondwana breaks up; the South Atlantic opens

ages.description: Mammals radiate into the niches left by the dinosaurs. A hot early Paleogene gives way to cooling, and an ice sheet forms on Antarctica.
keyEvents: Mammals diversify rapidly: early primates, horses and whales
Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (~56 Ma): rapid warming of ~5–8 °C
Early Eocene Climatic Optimum (~53–49 Ma): forests reach the poles
India collides with Asia and the Himalayas begin to rise
Eocene–Oligocene transition (~34 Ma): the Antarctic ice sheet forms
ages.vegetation: Tropical forests early; open woodlands and early grasslands later

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Hothouse early, cooling into an icehouse
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Continents near modern positions; Antarctica isolated

ages.description: The world keeps cooling and drying. Grasslands spread, grazing mammals thrive, and the first hominins appear in Africa.
keyEvents: Grasslands expand; C4 grasses spread in the late Miocene (~8–6 Ma)
Miocene Climatic Optimum (~17–15 Ma), then renewed cooling
First hominins (Sahelanthropus, ~7 Ma); Australopithecus by ~4 Ma
Messinian salinity crisis (~6 Ma): the Mediterranean partly dries up
Isthmus of Panama closes (~3 Ma); Northern Hemisphere ice sheets begin to grow
ages.vegetation: Grasslands and savannas; boreal forest and tundra appear

environmentalConditions.globalTemp: Cooling, with a mid-Miocene warm spell

ages.description: The ice ages. Ice sheets repeatedly advance and retreat, giant mammals roam, and humans spread across the globe.
keyEvents: Glacial–interglacial cycles: every ~41,000 years, then ~100,000 years after ~1 Ma
Ice-age megafauna: mammoths, woolly rhinos, giant ground sloths
Homo erectus (~1.9 Ma) spreads beyond Africa; Homo sapiens appears ~300,000 years ago
Last Glacial Maximum (~21,000 years ago): sea level ~120 m lower than today
Holocene (from 11,700 years ago): a warm interglacial; megafaunal extinctions
ages.vegetation: Modern biomes; tundra and steppe expand in glacials

environmentalConditions.seaLevel: Swinging between ~120 m below today and today's level
environmentalConditions.landCoverage: Modern; land bridges exposed during glacials
